title: WHERE IS THE LINE BETWEEN ROMANCE AND LUST?
paragraphs: WHERE IS THE LINE BETWEEN ROMANCE AND LUST?
The line is not simply whether you touched them. Jesus goes deeper: What are you training your heart to do with someone made in the image of God?
There is a moment almost nobody talks about.
Nothing “happened.”
At least, that is what you keep telling yourself.
You didn't sleep together.
You didn't technically commit adultery.
Maybe you didn't even kiss.
It was just a conversation that lasted too long.
A message you reread more times than you would admit.
A photograph you returned to.
A fantasy you allowed to finish.
A relationship that became emotionally intimate while remaining conveniently undefined.
A hand that stayed somewhere a little longer than necessary.
A late-night conversation that would have sounded very different if Jesus had been visibly sitting between you.
And somewhere inside, beneath the butterflies and chemistry and excitement, came the question:
Is this romance... or have I crossed into lust?
Maybe that question brought you here.
Then stay.
Because the most dangerous line between romance and lust may not be where your body finally goes.
It may be where your heart quietly decides what another human being is for.
And Jesus refuses to leave us guessing.
In Matthew 5:28, Christ says:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn...
The Greek text continues by saying that such a person has already committed adultery with her “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ” — en tē kardia autou — “in his heart.”
Do not rush past the wording.
Jesus is not teaching that merely noticing that another person is physically beautiful is identical to adultery. Nor is He declaring that every experience of attraction is itself sexual sin.

The construction includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai, expressing looking toward, or for the purpose of, desiring. The warning concerns more than the involuntary recognition that somebody is attractive. Christ penetrates into the intention of the gaze—the heart that looks in order to cultivate wrongful sexual desire.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Christianity is not anti-attraction.
Christianity is not anti-romance.
Christianity is not anti-body.
And Christianity is certainly not anti-marriage.

God invented all of those things before pornography, hookup culture, dating apps, secret messages, emotional affairs, situationships, and the thousand modern ways human beings learned to separate desire from covenant.

Scripture can speak about romantic love with astonishing intensity. Song of Songs describes love as strong as death, its passion fierce, its flames like fire, and says that many waters cannot quench it. The Bible is not embarrassed by romantic desire.
So the biblical question cannot simply be:
“Do I desire this person?”
The deeper question is:
“What is my desire trying to do to this person?”
That is where things become uncomfortable.
Romance says, I see you.
Lust says, I want to consume you.
Romance can admire beauty while remembering the soul inhabiting the body.
Lust slowly reduces the soul until the body becomes the point.
Romance asks how to honor.
Lust calculates how far it can go.
Romance can wait.
Lust keeps negotiating.
Romance wants truth.
Lust thrives in secrecy.
Romance sees a person whose holiness matters.
Lust sees a desire whose satisfaction matters.
And sometimes they feel almost identical at first.
That is why this is so dangerous.
Both can make your heart race.
Both can keep you awake.
Both can create anticipation.
Both can produce intense physical attraction.
Both can make you want closeness.
The difference is not necessarily the intensity of the fire.
The difference is what the fire is allowed to burn.
Godly romantic desire can say:
I want you badly enough that I refuse to use you.
Lust says:
I want you badly enough that I will keep finding theological excuses to take what does not belong to me.
Read that again.
Because sometimes the sentence Christians need most is the sentence they least want to hear.
You can put worship music behind lust.
You can call lust “chemistry.”
You can call lust “love.”
You can call emotional dependency “God brought us together.”
You can call compromised boundaries “we're serious about each other.”
You can pray before crossing a boundary and still cross a boundary.
Religious vocabulary does not sanctify disobedience.
And perhaps the most revealing question is not, “How far can we go before it becomes sin?”
Maybe the question should be:
“How close can I bring this person to Christ without making myself an obstacle between them and Him?”
Imagine that.
Imagine dating someone and deciding that their relationship with Jesus matters more to you than satisfying your immediate appetite.
Imagine wanting somebody and still being willing to hear the word no.
Imagine being attracted without demanding possession.
Imagine being affectionate without turning affection into manipulation.
Imagine refusing to awaken desires you have no righteous intention or covenantal freedom to fulfill.
Imagine praying:
Jesus, if having this person requires becoming someone who dishonors You, I would rather lose the relationship than lose obedience.
That prayer separates romance from idolatry very quickly.
Because sometimes what we call “love” is actually terror.
Terror of loneliness.
Terror that nobody else will choose us.
Terror that if we establish boundaries, the person will leave.
So we compromise.
Just a little.
Then another little.
And another.
Until one night we discover that the line did not suddenly move.
We did.
Perhaps you know that feeling.
You promised God you wouldn't go there again.
Then you went there again.
You deleted it.
Then searched for it again.
You said the conversation was innocent.
But you knew why you kept checking whether they were online.
You told yourself the relationship was “complicated.”
But somewhere beneath the complications was something painfully simple:
You wanted something God had not given you permission to take.
And afterward came the shame.
That awful silence after desire has gotten what it demanded.
The screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet.
The adrenaline disappears.
And suddenly you can hear your conscience again.
Maybe you whispered:
“God... I'm sorry.”
Maybe this has happened so many times that even saying sorry feels fraudulent now.
You wonder whether repentance still counts when you have repented before.
You wonder whether Jesus has become tired of watching you crawl back from the same battlefield.
You wonder whether somebody who genuinely loves Christ could struggle with thoughts like yours.
This is where the Gospel must interrupt the story.
Because Jesus did not expose lust in Matthew 5 so that broken sinners would become better at hiding.
He exposed the heart because He came to redeem the heart.
Christ does not merely want to stop your hands.
He wants to transform your desires.
He does not merely say, “Behave.”
He says, in effect, Come into the light.
The cross means your sexual sin is neither insignificant nor unforgivable.
Both truths must remain together.
Sin is serious enough that Christ died.
Grace is powerful enough that Christ died for sinners.
There is therefore no need to rename lust in order to receive mercy.
You can call it what God calls it.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can turn around.
You can establish boundaries that your old self would have mocked.
You can end conversations that keep feeding fantasy.
You can stop treating pornography like a harmless private habit.
You can stop flirting with somebody else's spouse.
You can stop maintaining an emotionally intimate relationship you would panic to have exposed.
You can stop asking how close to the cliff Christianity allows you to stand.
Not because boundaries save you.
Jesus saves you.
But the person who has encountered grace no longer wants to keep making peace with the chains from which Christ came to free them.
And there is another side of this that desperately needs saying.
Purity is not disgust with sexuality.
Some Christians were taught to fear their own bodies so thoroughly that attraction itself became associated with shame.
That is not the whole biblical picture either.
Song of Songs will not allow us to pretend marital desire is dirty. Scripture speaks unapologetically of powerful romantic love.
Biblical purity is not the absence of desire.
It is desire brought under the lordship of Christ.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire on the curtains can destroy it.
The problem was never that fire was hot.
The question was always whether the fire remained where it belonged.
And Paul gives us another devastating test for the heart.
When describing love in 1 Corinthians 13:5, the Greek says:
“οὐ ζητεῖ τὰ ἑαυτῆς” — ou zētei ta heautēs.
Literally, love does not seek “its own”; translations appropriately express the thought as love not insisting upon its own way or not being self-seeking.
Now place that beside lust.
Lust seeks its own.
Love asks, How can I honor you?
Lust asks, How can you satisfy me?
Love can sacrifice gratification for another person's good.
Lust tends to sacrifice another person's good for gratification.
That does not mean genuine romantic relationships contain no sexual desire. In marriage, sexual desire can be a beautiful dimension of covenant love.
It means desire must learn to kneel before love.
And love must kneel before Christ.
So where exactly is the line?
It is not reducible to a universal measurement of inches between two bodies.
Scripture gives commands, principles, and a vision of holiness deeper than a technical chart of permissible physical contact.

The line becomes visible when desire begins training you to use rather than honor; when imagination deliberately cultivates what God forbids; when affection becomes a strategy for sexual access; when secrecy becomes necessary; when another person's body becomes more valuable to you than their obedience to Christ; when you continually ask, “What can I get away with?” instead of, “What would glorify Jesus?”
And if you are reading this while thinking about one particular person...
you probably know why.
Not because every relationship you question is sinful.
But because conscience has a way of becoming painfully specific.
Maybe God is not asking you to stop loving them.
Maybe He is teaching you how to love them.
Without consuming them.
Without worshiping them.
Without needing them to become your savior.
Without making their body medicine for your loneliness.
Without demanding from dating what belongs to marriage.
Without calling obsession devotion.
Without calling possession love.
And perhaps real romance begins when you can look into the eyes of somebody you deeply desire and quietly decide:
Your soul matters more than my appetite.
That is rare.
That is beautiful.
That is costly.
And that begins to resemble Christ.
Because Jesus did not look at broken humanity and ask what He could extract from us.
He gave Himself for us.
Christian love ultimately takes its shape from a Savior who sacrifices rather than consumes.
So if this article uncovered something you have kept hidden, don't perform.
Don't pretend.
Take it to Jesus.
Confess specifically.
Repent honestly.
Remove what needs removing.
End what needs ending.
Confess to a trustworthy mature believer where accountability is needed.
Seek pastoral help where the pattern has become deeply entrenched.
And if you fall, do not turn failure into permission to stay on the ground.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
Not casually.
Not presumptuously.
But believing that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the scandal you brought into the light.
This is what we mean when we say:
Not scandal denied.
Not sin celebrated.
Not holiness abandoned.
Scandal confessed.
Sin confronted.
Grace received.
A sinner transformed.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not for performance.
As a small public declaration that you are done pretending darkness is freedom.
Send this privately if that would protect their dignity.
There may come a night when the emotions are louder than your convictions, and you need to remember why you established the boundary in the first place.
It doesn't. We glorify God through faith expressed in obedience, love, generosity, and faithful stewardship—not by purchasing spiritual status.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help that work continue reaching people.
Not because sharing makes you righteous.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
Maybe they don't need another seductive algorithm tonight.
Maybe they need truth.
Maybe they need permission to confess.
Maybe they need to discover that holiness is not God stealing something beautiful from them.
Maybe holiness is God refusing to let something beautiful destroy them.
And maybe the question they have been asking is finally about to change.
Not:
“Where is the line so I can get as close as possible?”
But:
“Jesus, how close can I get to You?”
Because eventually every romance reaches its deepest test.
Not how intensely you wanted them.
Not how many butterflies you felt.
Not how long you stayed awake talking.
Not whether everybody thought you looked perfect together.
But whether loving them taught you to become more faithful to Christ—or whether wanting them slowly taught you how to disobey Him.
And when desire begins screaming, remember this:
The person you are tempted to consume is a soul Jesus calls you to love—and sometimes the holiest proof that you love them is what you refuse to take from them.
